In the same deterministic-repair pass (manifest tool `axiom-encode repair-eitc-section-152-import`) it also re-grounds `eitc_maximum` on the imported Rev. Proc. 2025-32 published maximum-credit table instead of recomputing credit percentage x earned income amount (the companion test expectation moves from 4426.8 to 4427), and rewrites `eitc_phased_in` to return that maximum at or above the earned income amount and to floor earned income at zero below it.

modules.description_quote: Encode section 152(c) for EITC
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: unclear: the file did not exist at the parent commit (1bc40147, which has no statutes/26/152* file at all), so there is no pre-fix encoding that could disagree with the source; this is a net-new encoding of 26 USC 152(c), not a correction.
modules.triage_notes: Status is 'added' — verified with `git ls-tree -r --name-only 1bc40147... -- statutes/26` that no 152 module existed before. All nine rules are new (parameters 1/2, 1/2, 19, 24; derived relationship, age, pre-tiebreaker, tiebreaker, and combined qualifying_child), with effective_from 1990-01-01 and proof atoms citing us/statute/26/152. It supplies the definition that 32.yaml had been taking as an opaque input, so it is the vehicle for re-grounding that input, but per the 'adds scope the module never claimed' guidance it is added precision rather than a corrected meaning. Recommend a reviewer prune index 0 from a defect corpus: the only defect evidence in this commit lives in index 1. Provision text for 26 USC 152 was not separately resolved; the module summary quotes it in full and matches the encoded structure.

modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: eitc_maximum recomputed the maximum credit as credit percentage x earned income amount (13020 * 0.34 = 4426.8; 18290 * 0.45 = 8230.5), so the encoded maximum disagreed with the Rev. Proc. 2025-32 maximum-credit amounts the module already imports (4427 and 8231), and eitc_phased_in inherited the same understatement at and above the earned income amount.
modules.triage_notes: Decisive numeric evidence is in the companion test, statutes/26/32.test.yaml: `us:statutes/26/32#eitc_maximum: 4426.8` changes to `4427` in this commit, so the module's output value really changed. Checked the imported authority: policies/irs/rev-proc-2025-32/earned-income-credit.yaml publishes eitc_maximum_credit_amounts {0: 664, 1: 4427, 2: 7316, 3: 8231} against eitc_earned_income_amounts {0: 8680, 1: 13020, 2: 18290, 3: 18290}; rate x amount gives 664.02, 4426.8, 7316.0, 8230.5, so the pre-fix formula disagreed with the published table for three of four child counts. History: the table lookup was the original encoding (c3720e620) and was replaced by the rate x amount formula in b3801ee4e 'Regenerate validated US RuleSpec encodings' (an openai gpt-5.5 backend run per the manifest); this commit restores it, so the defect was introduced by that regeneration. This commit's 32.yaml change is a deterministic repair (manifest: backend 'deterministic', model 'eitc-section-152-import-v1', tool 'axiom-encode repair-eitc-section-152-import'). NO quotable description exists: the commit body is empty, the subject only mentions the 152(c) encode, prep_commit found no PR (pr is null), and the diff contains no comments — this is exactly the screen flag (subject says Encode, diff also rewrites 32.yaml), which is why confidence sits in the 0.5-0.79 band despite the diff and test being unambiguous. Two other changes ride along in the same module and a reviewer should decide whether to split them out: (a) eitc_phased_in gains `if earned_income >= eitc_earned_income_amount: eitc_maximum`, which is the same amount correction propagated to the phase-in plateau, plus a `max(0, earned_income)` floor that has no added proof atom and no clause in the quoted 32(a)(1) text ('the credit percentage of so much of the taxpayer's earned income for the taxable year as does not exceed the earned income amount') — a sensible non-negativity guard but not a cited-source correction; (b) eitc_qualifying_child's formula swaps the free input qualifying_child_under_section_152_c_as_modified_for_eitc for the new derived eitc_qualifying_child_base, which is added grounding/precision rather than a corrected meaning. Provision read: resolve_provision.py on us/statute/26/32 returned 16,971 chars and confirms 32(a)(1), 32(a)(2)(A) and the (b)(1)/(b)(2) tables as quoted above.

verdict.justification: I refute the "unclear" hold: for this module the evidence does settle it. `statutes/26/152/c.yaml` is created by this commit (`new file mode 100644`, `@@ -0,0 +1,237 @@`, pre_lines 0), and I independently confirmed with `git ls-tree -r 1bc40147 --name-only statutes/26 | grep 152` that the parent tree contains no 152 file at all, so there is no renamed or relocated predecessor whose meaning could have disagreed with 26 USC 152(c). The commit's `--stat` shows it deletes no other rule module (only 32.yaml is modified, and its diff removes no rules), so no prior 152(c) encoding was folded in here; the parent 32.yaml simply left `qualifying_child_under_section_152_c_as_modified_for_eitc` as an unresolved leaf input rather than encoding it wrongly. This module change is therefore new coverage the module never claimed, not a correction of encoded meaning.

+++ b/statutes/26/152/c.yaml
@@ -0,0 +1,237 @@
verdict.notes:
Scope note: the real fidelity content of commit 682af97f25 sits in module index 1 (statutes/26/32.yaml), which should be adjudicated on its own. There the diff replaces `- eitc_phase_in_rate * eitc_earned_income_amount` with a Rev. Proc. table lookup (`match eitc_capped_child_count: 0 => eitc_maximum_credit_amounts[0] ...`) and replaces `- eitc_phase_in_rate * min(earned_income, eitc_earned_income_amount)` with `if earned_income >= eitc_earned_income_amount: eitc_maximum else: eitc_phase_in_rate * min(max(0, earned_income), eitc_earned_income_amount)`; it also adds `eitc_qualifying_child_base`, which deliberately omits the 152(c)(1)(D) support test per the quoted 32(c)(3)(A) text "determined without regard to paragraph (1)(D) thereof and section 152(e)". verdict.justification: The pre-fix formula `eitc_phase_in_rate * eitc_earned_income_amount` is a verbatim implementation of the text the rule's own proof atom cites — 26 USC 32(a)(2)(A), "the credit percentage of the earned income amount" — and the resolved provision text confirms that section 32 states no maximum-credit dollar amount anywhere, while its rounding rule at 32(j)(2) reaches only "any dollar amount in subsection (b)(2)(A)" and (i)(1), never the credit ceiling. The numbers the first reader treats as the correct source values (4427, 8231) exist only in the IRS's published Rev. Proc. 2025-32 table, which is the same product rounded to whole dollars in both directions: 13020*0.34 = 4426.80 → 4427 but 8680*0.0765 = 664.02 → 664, so the published column is a rounding presentation, not an independent legal amount that the statutory product contradicts. Switching to the table is therefore a rounding-convention choice (and it is a revert — the original encoding c3720e620 used the table, the b3801ee4e regeneration switched to the product), worth at most $0.50 and pointing in both directions; it is not a numeric value that was wrong versus the cited source.

verdict.notes:
Evidence read: bundle JSON, diffs/us/682af97f25/001.diff, pre/post statutes/26/32.yaml at 1bc40147ba and 682af97f25, statutes/26/32.test.yaml diff, policies/irs/rev-proc-2025-32/earned-income-credit.yaml, and the pinned provision text for us/statute/26/32 (corpus release us-rulespec-2026-07-13).

1. No message evidence at all. The commit subject is "Encode section 152(c) for EITC" with an empty body and no PR; the first reader's quote field is empty with source "none". Every part of the amount_mismatch claim is inference from the diff.

2. The commit is predominantly a feature commit. Its substantive change is `eitc_qualifying_child`: the stub input `qualifying_child_under_section_152_c_as_modified_for_eitc` is replaced by a new derived `eitc_qualifying_child_base` that imports the newly encoded statutes/26/152/c. That is coverage the module never claimed to encode (it had punted to an assumed input), which the rubric says is not a defect.

3. The change arguably moves eitc_maximum AWAY from the statute. Post-fix the rule still carries the unchanged proof atom `text: "the credit percentage of the earned income amount"` while the formula now returns an imported Rev. Proc. table cell, and `eitc_maximum` feeds the 32(a)(2) limitation directly at line 463 of the post file: `max(0, min(eitc_phased_in, eitc_maximum - eitc_reduction))`. The statutory ceiling in (a)(2)(A) is the exact product, so the post-fix encoding puts a rounded IRS display figure inside a statutory computation.

4. Intent is nevertheless deliberate: statutes/26/32.test.yaml changes `us:statutes/26/32#eitc_maximum: 4426.8` to `us:statutes/26/32#eitc_maximum: 4427`. So the maintainer chose the published table. A reviewer whose convention is "an imported, cited Rev. Proc. table governs the annual dollar amounts" could legitimately reclassify this to confirmed/amount_mismatch. That convention question, not a factual dispute, is what separates my verdict from the first reader's; I did not find it settled anywhere in the module or repo.

5. One genuinely separate item the first reader folded into "inherited the same understatement": eitc_phased_in gains `max(0, earned_income)`. With negative earned income (self-employment loss) the pre-fix formula returned a negative phased-in credit, which no reading of 32(a)(1) supports. That is a real, if small and undocumented, meaning correction — but it sits in a different rule than the candidate's rule_path (rules[eitc_maximum].versions[0].formula) and is not amount_mismatch; it is a missing floor. The companion `if earned_income >= eitc_earned_income_amount: eitc_maximum` branch is purely downstream bookkeeping to keep phased_in equal to the new table maximum at the kink, not an independent fidelity fix.

Recommendation: drop this case, or, if kept, re-scope it to the eitc_phased_in negative-earnings floor rather than the eitc_maximum rounding revert. A $0.20 (0.005%) discrepancy that flips sign across table rows is a weak training example of amount_mismatch.

verdict.justification: I tried to refute this as a mere re-encode or as an entity/scope change, and could not: the decisive meaning change is the deletion of a formula that decided the §63(f)(3) "$750 for $600" substitution by testing an undeclared free input against bare integers (`filing_status == 0 or filing_status == 3`), with no enum, import, or in-module declaration giving those codes meaning, while its proof atoms claimed the statutory excerpt "In the case of an individual who is not married and is not a surviving spouse" as grounding. The pinned corpus text confirms §63(f)(3) states the test as "not married and is not a surviving spouse" and §63(g) routes marital status to §7703 (surviving spouse comes from §2(a)) — nothing in 26 USC 63 supplies a filing-status code; the fix removes the branch and defers the output, blocked by exactly those two provisions. The competing kind wrong_entity_or_scope does not fit better: the spouse rules move from TaxUnit booleans to a Person relation but the TaxUnit output surface is preserved via `count_where(...) > 0`, so that is added precision the module never claimed rather than a corrected entity, and the removal of `additional_standard_deduction_amount_under_subsection_f` is a downstream consequence of the deferral, not an independent scope correction. The parallel replacement of the assumed local input `additional_exemption_allowable_for_spouse_under_section_151_b` with a hashed import of `us:statutes/26/151#exemption_individual_eligible` is the same defect family (ungrounded assumption re-grounded), which reinforces untraceable_branch over the alternatives.

verdict.justification: The refutation attempt fails on both prongs: the diff changes executable meaning (two formulas plus a new gating rule and new inputs), and the pre-fix encoding gave answers that contradict the cited text rather than merely lacking coverage. The pinned release shows 63(c)(1) defines the standard deduction "Except as otherwise provided in this subsection" as basic + additional, 63(c)(3) defines the additional standard deduction as "the sum of each additional amount to which the taxpayer is entitled under subsection (f)" (which includes 63(f)(2)'s blind amount), and 63(c)(6) says "the standard deduction shall be zero" for MFS-where-either-spouse-itemizes, nonresident aliens, 443(a)(1) short-period filers, and estates/trusts/common trust funds/partnerships. Both added pieces are missing statutory conditions, so unrepresented_clause is the right kind; no other kind (amount, boundary, polarity, entity, period) is the root of either change.

modules.triage_notes: Recommend a reviewer prune this one. (1) Semantics: pre-fix `if household_size > 8: table[8] + (hh-8)*additional else: table[hh]` and post-fix `table[max(min(hh,8),1)] + max(hh-8,0)*additional` are mathematically identical for all hh >= 1; the only behavioral delta is hh <= 0, which previously raised a missing-parameter error and now silently returns table[1] = 298 — a value the source does not state for a zero-person household, so the fix is not more source-faithful there, just non-erroring. (2) Source WAS read through the pinned corpus release (us/guidance/usda/fns/snap-fy2026-cola/page-1): 'Household Size ... 1 $298 ... 8 $1,789 ... Each Additional Member $218'. Table covers only sizes 1-8, so the pre-fix `> 8` boundary matches the source; this is NOT boundary_direction in the fidelity sense despite the screen description calling it a 'boundary fix'. (3) Evidence that large households already worked: the companion test policies/usda/snap/fy-2026-cola/maximum-allotments.test.yaml contains `household_size: 9 -> snap_maximum_allotment: 2007` (= 1789 + 218), it was added two commits earlier in 29176b846 together with the pre-fix formula, and this commit did NOT touch the test file (git diff 689b7b5ada 79be93e456 on the .test.yaml is empty). So the pre-fix encoding demonstrably produced the source-stated amount for a 9-person household. (4) The only mechanism by which the pre-fix form could fail for sizes >8: axiom-rules-engine's dense executor evaluates both branches of an If eagerly (src/dense.rs ~line 2130: `then_values` and `else_values` are both computed then masked) and lookup_parameter_dense (src/dense.rs ~line 3288) returns EvalError::MissingParameterValue for an unknown key, so `table[9]` in the dead else-branch would abort the batch; the scalar engine (src/engine.rs ~line 794) short-circuits and is unaffected. That is an engine-robustness concern, not a source-fidelity one. (5) Commit body is empty and there is no PR for this commit (bundle pr == null), so the subject line is the only quotable evidence and it is generic about the defect. (6) No unrelated changes: 2 insertions / 3 deletions, one rule, no proof/parameter/effective-date churn. (7) Follow-up noted: the next commit on this file, 901aeb85d 'Move SNAP regular allotment formula to USC', is purely additive (adds snap_one_person_thrifty_food_plan_cost and statutes/7/2017/a.yaml) and does not revert or re-ground this formula. (8) Classification judgment: 'mechanical' does not literally fit because the formula text changed, but the change preserves meaning over the entire valid domain and only adds robustness the module never claimed, which the task instructions say to classify 'unclear at most'.

verdict.justification: The pinned provision (us/guidance/usda/fns/snap-fy2026-cola/page-1) states 298/546/785/994/1183/1421/1571/1789 for sizes 1-8 and "Each Additional Member $218", and I evaluated both formulas over sizes 0-20: they return identical values for every household size the source defines (1 and up), differing only at household_size 0, where the post-fix clamp invents $298 for a size the USDA table never contemplates. No parameter value, version window, effective date, entity, period, or branch selection changed — the `> 8` test and the clamped `min(...,8)` pick the same amount at 8, 9 and above — so nothing in the encoded meaning moved toward or away from the source. The commit says "safe", not "correct", and there is no source basis for calling the old formula wrong; the motivation is engine-side (axiom-rules-engine src/dense.rs evaluates both `If` branches over the whole batch and `lookup_parameter_dense` hard-errors with MissingParameterValue on an out-of-range key, while src/engine.rs's scalar `If` is lazy). That makes this an evaluator-robustness refactor, not a fidelity correction, so the first reader's "other" kind should not be retained as a defect kind at all.

+          snap_maximum_allotment_table[max(min(household_size, 8), 1)]
verdict.notes: Refutation attempt found no fidelity kind that survives. boundary_direction fails: both forms give table[8] at size 8 and table[8]+218 at size 9, so no strictness or direction changed. amount_mismatch fails: no number in the diff, and the module's parameter tables and $218 additional-member value are byte-identical before and after and match the provision text exactly. unrepresented_clause fails: the "Each Additional Member" clause was already encoded in the pre-fix if-branch. polarity_or_logic fails: the correct branch always fired; the if/else was replaced by arithmetic, not corrected. wrong_entity_or_scope fails: entity Household, period Month, dtype Money, effective_from 2025-10-01 all unchanged. The one genuine counter-argument for keeping it, which a reviewer should weigh: in the engine's dense/batch path both branches are evaluated eagerly (src/dense.rs CompiledScalarExpr::If evaluates then_expr and else_expr then selects, and lookup_parameter_dense returns EvalError::MissingParameterValue for any key not in the table, failing the entire batch), so pre-fix a microsim batch containing any 9+-person household would abort rather than return the source-stated amount. That is a real executability bug against a population the source covers, which is why the commit names large households — but it is an engine-interaction failure, not an encoded meaning that disagrees with the USDA table, and the harness's own definition of a fidelity defect ("an encoded meaning that disagrees with the cited source text") excludes it; the first reader's own other_kind string concedes this ("not a disagreement with the source text"). Note also that the fix's only behavioral change against the old formula is the unsourced $298 for household_size 0, i.e. it adds a value with no source basis rather than restoring one. Commit touches one file, 2 insertions / 3 deletions, no companion test added for the 9+ case, no proof-hash or metadata churn. Recommendation: prune from a fidelity-defect corpus, or keep only in a separate evaluation-safety bucket.

Provision WAS read through the pinned corpus path us-co/regulation/10-ccr-2506-1/4.408 (release us-rulespec-2026-07-13, no toolchain pin existed at this commit so the resolver fell back, fallback_index 4): 4.408(B) reads 'Households that do not meet expanded or basic categorical eligibility criteria shall have their nonexempt resources, as anticipated to be available in the issuance month, used to determine household eligibility. The resources of a sponsor and spouse considered toward a non-citizen household shall be the sponsor's total resources less two thousand dollars ($2,000).' The pre-fix symbol name therefore mirrors the source's own wording, which is why I did not call this fidelity: a judge comparing the pre-fix module to 4.408 alone would see nothing wrong. What the fix actually corrects is a dangling/ungrounded input - `nonexempt_resources` appears nowhere else in the repo at the parent (verified by git grep at 0fda5d6f), while `snap_countable_resources` is derived in 4.409.yaml (added by 93e825e90, present at the parent). Not mechanical: a formula input changed, which the mechanical definition excludes. Two caveats for a reviewer: (1) the 4.408 version is effective_from 2024-10-01 but every 4.409 rule, including snap_countable_resources, is effective_from 2025-10-01, so the post-fix dependency has no version covering Oct 2024 - Sep 2025; (2) 4.409's snap_countable_resources sums liquid + non-liquid equity + jointly owned + commingled and never nets out the section 4.410 exemptions (4.410 is not encoded in this repo at this commit), so the fix equates 'nonexempt' with 4.409 'countable'. The PR attached in the bundle (rulespec-us #395) is the later monorepo-consolidation PR that absorbed rulespec-us-co history; it says nothing about this commit, and has no reviews or review comments. The commit body is empty, so the only quotable text is the subject. Related later wiring commit noticed in history: e3f7c3741 'Wire SNAP resource eligibility upstream'.

verdict.justification: The cited provision itself says households "shall have their nonexempt resources, as anticipated to be available in the issuance month, used to determine household eligibility," so the pre-fix leaf input `nonexempt_resources` was the provision's own term and did not disagree with 10 CCR 2506-1 4.408(B); the derivation of resource components lives in the separate section 4.409, which 4.408 never claimed to encode. The git history shows this is a wiring step, not a correction: 4fb47b2af added 4.408 when no 4.409 module existed, 93e825e90 added 4.409 (defining `snap_countable_resources`) minutes earlier the same day, and ca02796d40 connects the two. Nothing about encoded meaning relative to the source moved - every test value is byte-identical (100000, 4500, 2600) with unchanged expected outputs, and only the input identifier was renamed. Under the rule that added precision or scope a module never claimed is not a defect, this is an integration refactor rather than a fidelity defect.

Tension a reviewer must settle: computed outputs are unchanged — statutes/26/63/c.test.yaml still asserts standard_deduction of 16100/33850/35500/26200 and only drops now-imported intermediate outputs — so this is a re-grounding of provenance plus a structural move, not a numeric correction. It is more than the rubric's 'citation-string-only' mechanical case (four rules are deleted from the module and the summary's claim that the statute states 2026 amounts is withdrawn), and it matches untraceable_branch's 'values with no basis in the cited source ... the fix removes or re-grounds it'. A judge reading only the pre-fix file against 26 USC 63(c) can find the defect, which is what makes it corpus-worthy; a stricter reviewer could still call it mechanical provenance. The rest of the diff is cosmetic (§ -> 'section' in source strings). This commit sits in a run of sibling 'Move ... upstream/to USC' commits (901aeb85d, c301d68a4, 23ff66987), i.e. a systematic re-grounding campaign rather than a one-off bug fix. Later commits kept reworking these files (2175d5239 'Re-encode 26 USC 63(c) with upstream dependencies', 23f5c1736 'Use corpus source verification for guidance values').

modules.description_quote: Annual inflation-adjusted dollar amounts are imported from the IRS tax-year authority, not encoded in the statute file.

verdict.justification: This candidate module is a brand-new file (0 pre-lines, "new file mode 100644", "--- /dev/null"), so it has no pre-fix encoded meaning that could disagree with a source, and nothing inside it is removed or re-grounded — it is the destination half of the commit, not the carrier of the defect. Every value it introduces is byte-identical to a value deleted from statutes/26/63/c.yaml and statutes/26/63/c/5.yaml in the same commit, and statutes/26/63/c.test.yaml shows the composed outputs are unchanged (standard_deduction stays 16100 / 33850 / 35500 / 26200), so this file corrects no number, boundary, clause, window, or branch. The real untraceable_branch defect is verifiable but sits in the other two modules: the pinned release (us-rulespec-2026-07-13, corpus commit 612d20ca) shows IRC 63(c) states "$4,400 in the case of a head of household", "$3,000 in any other case", the 63(c)(7)(A) substitutions of "$23,625" and "$15,750", and 63(c)(5)'s "(A) $500, or (B) the sum of $250", and never 16100/32200/24150/1350/450 that the statute modules attributed to it. Scored as its own case this file is new coverage the module never previously claimed, which the rubric puts at unclear-at-most; because the added content is correct and additive rather than corrective, not_a_defect is the accurate call for module index 0.

verdict.notes: Do not drop the commit — relabel which module carries it. Keep statutes/26/63/c.yaml (module index 1) and statutes/26/63/c/5.yaml (module index 2) as untraceable_branch fidelity cases: their decisive deleted lines are "source: IRC §63(c)(2) as amended 2026" over values 0: 16100 / 1: 32200 / 2: 16100 / 3: 24150, "source: IRC §63(f)(1) as amended 2026" over 0: 2050 / 1: 1650 / 2: 1650 / 3: 2050, and "source: 26 USC 63(c)(5)(B)" over formula: '1350' and formula: '450'. The pinned corpus text refutes all of those attributions (statute carries $4,400/$3,000, the 63(c)(7)(A) substitutions "$23,625"/"$15,750", and 63(c)(5)(A)/(B) "$500"/"the sum of $250"), so the kind untraceable_branch ("formulas grounded on the wrong provision") is right for the commit — I could not refute the kind, only its assignment to this file. Two caveats for the reviewer. (1) A dissent is available even on modules 1-2: no computed value changes anywhere in the commit, so someone applying the rubric's "excerpt-only and citation-string-only corrections are mechanical (provenance)" line could call the whole commit provenance bookkeeping; I think untraceable_branch still wins there because whole rules (not just citation strings) are deleted from the statute namespace and the statute verifiably never stated those amounts. (2) The only genuine meaning delta the new file introduces is a filing_status == 4 (surviving spouse) arm in additional_standard_deduction_per_condition_amount that the deleted 0-3 table never had — added scope, not a correction — and its sibling basic_standard_deduction_amount match still has arms only for 1/2/3/0 with no 4 arm, despite IRC 63(c)(2)(A)(ii) giving a surviving spouse the 200-percent (joint) amount. That inconsistency is newly authored code in this commit, not a repair, so it does not make this module a defect fix; it is a candidate for a separate, later fidelity case if a subsequent commit adds the missing arm.

verdict.justification: Nothing in statutes/26/63/c.yaml changes encoded meaning: the four removed rules reappear verbatim in the added policies/irs/rev-proc-2025-32/standard-deduction.yaml with identical values (16100/32200/16100/24150, 1650/2050) and identical effective_from '2026-01-01', the surviving rules differ only in cosmetic source strings ("-    source: IRC §63(f)(1)(A)" / "+    source: IRC section 63(f)(1)(A)"), and every substantive test expectation is a context line — us:statutes/26/63/c#standard_deduction stays 16100/33850/35500/26200 before and after. The pre-fix amounts were also not wrong against the source the reader cites: §63(c)(2)'s post-2017 substitutions of $15,750/$31,500/$23,625 plus the §63(c)(4) inflation adjustment for years after 2025 are exactly what produce 16100/32200/24150, so the numbers were statutorily grounded and only the pinpoint citation was imprecise (statute rather than the revenue procedure that publishes the indexed figure). verdict.notes:
Decisive evidence, all read directly: (1) diff 001.diff removes basic_standard_deduction_table/_amount and additional_standard_deduction_per_condition_table/_amount from statutes/26/63/c.yaml; (2) `git show 34ad146770:policies/irs/rev-proc-2025-32/standard-deduction.yaml` re-declares the same numerals (16100, 32200, 16100, 24150, 1650, 2050) at the same effective_from '2026-01-01'; (3) statutes/26/63/c.test.yaml keeps every standard_deduction expectation unchanged (16100/33850/35500/26200) and only drops assertions for the rules that moved modules. No formula, value, version window, effective date, boolean logic, or computed output changed. The only module-level change beyond relocation is that basic_standard_deduction_amount and additional_standard_deduction_per_condition_amount are no longer this module's output surface — a refactor, not a meaning correction.

Fallback if the reviewer disagrees with not_a_defect: the correct bucket is "mechanical" (provenance), per the rule that citation-string/attribution corrections are provenance, not fidelity — it should NOT be "fidelity / untraceable_branch" either way. I did not pick mechanical as the primary verdict only because the literal mechanical criteria require parameters and outputs to stay the same in the file, and here four parameter/derived rules left the module.

Caveat I could not close: `resolve_provision.py` cannot read 26 USC 63 through the pinned releases ("Unsupported corpus document class '26'", no_toolchain_corpus_pin across all us-* releases), so my statement of §63(c)(2)/(c)(4) content relies on the first reader's own quoted statutory text plus the arithmetic (15750→16100, 31500→32200, 23625→24150), not on a corpus read. If a reviewer treats "the parameter's source string names a provision that does not literally contain the numeral" as itself a fidelity defect, that reading is available — but it is an attribution error, and the fix changes no encoded meaning.

Separate observation, out of scope for module index 1: the added IRS module's additional_standard_deduction_per_condition_amount branches on filing_status 4 (surviving spouse), which the old indexed table (keys 0–3 only) never covered. That is new coverage the statute module never claimed, not a corrected defect.

verdict.notes: Flip condition for a reviewer: if source attribution counts as encoded meaning in this corpus (Axiom's grounding regime arguably treats it that way), then the first reader's untraceable_branch label is the right fidelity kind, since the deleted rules asserted that 26 USC 63(c)(5)(B) supplies $1,350 and 26 USC 63(c)(2) supplies $16,100 while the repo's own new module states these are "tax year 2026 inflation-adjusted standard deduction amounts" published by Rev. Proc. 2025-32 section 3.14 — both cannot be the primary authority for the same figure, and the flat minimum was attributed to subparagraph (B) rather than (A). Two caveats on the strict-mechanical reading: the diff deletes three parameter rules and adds an `imports:` edge, which is more than the enumerated "citation-path strings" case and breaks any external reference to us:statutes/26/63/c/5#dependent_minimum; and the sibling module in the same commit (statutes/26/63/c.yaml) did change test expectations, so the commit as a whole is not purely mechanical even though this module is. I could not verify the statutory face amounts through the pinned corpus: resolve_provision returned {"error": "unresolved", "selection_basis": "no_toolchain_corpus_pin"} for every citation form tried ("26/63/c/5", "usc/26/63/c/5", "26 USC 63(c)(5)"), and sources/slices/ in rulespec-us at this commit carries only 7-USC and USDA SNAP slices — no title 26 text. These 26/63 modules also carry no corpus_citation_path and no encoding manifest, which is worth noting if the corpus is meant to sample encoder-produced modules.

triage.commit_summary: The commit replaces Colorado SNAP utility-allowance selection in 10 CCR 2506-1 4.407.31 — which had dispatched the four allowance amounts on an undeclared caller-supplied `snap_utility_allowance_type` string ("SUA"/"LUA"/"OUA"/"IUA") — with five new derived rules that encode the 4.407.31(A)-(D) eligibility conditions themselves (qualifying heating/cooling cost, LEAP/E-EBT payment in the prior 12 months, landlord-billed or shared or public-housing excess or irregular heating/cooling cost; a count of non-heating/cooling utility costs; and the >=2 / exactly-1 / telephone-only branches). The four money rules now key off those derived eligibility judgments instead of the input, and both companion test files were rewritten to drive the module from raw utility-cost facts.

modules.description_quote: Households receive only one of the four allowances. HCUA applies when the household has a qualifying heating or cooling cost, prior 12-month LEAP or E-EBT payment, qualifying landlord-billed heating or cooling charge, shared heating or cooling cost, public-housing excess heating or cooling cost, or irregular heating or cooling cost between billing periods.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The four allowance rules cited 4.407.31(A)-(D) as their source but encoded none of the (A)-(D) qualifying conditions, instead paying the amount whenever a caller asserted an allowance-type code, so a household that actually met the regulation's heating/cooling or utility-count conditions got $0 unless the caller supplied the right string, and a household that met none of them got the full allowance if the caller said so.
modules.triage_notes: Single-module commit; both companion tests (regulations/10-ccr-2506-1/4.407.31.test.yaml and policies/cdhs/snap/fy-2026-benefit-calculation.test.yaml) were rewritten to feed raw utility-cost facts, and the policy test's expected shelter/allotment numbers moved ($182 -> $298) because the scenario household now qualifies for the $594 HCUA. Verified with `git grep snap_utility_allowance_type` at parent 8076145: the string was never defined by any rule in the repo pre-fix, so the 4.407.31(A)-(D) selection clauses existed nowhere in the encoding — this is a missing-clause fidelity gap, not a refactor of an existing encoded condition. Confidence held at 0.7 because the commit body is empty (subject only: "Derive Colorado SNAP utility allowance") and the bundle's PR (#395) is the unrelated us monorepo-absorption PR, so no maintainer or reviewer text names the defect. Source text NOT read: the module carries only a source_url (no corpus citation path; corpus_citation_paths_seen is empty and the repo at this commit has no .axiom/toolchain.toml), and resolve_provision.py returned {"error":"unresolved","selection_basis":"no_toolchain_corpus_pin"} for every candidate release — so the exact wording of (A)-(D) (e.g. whether OUA truly requires exactly one non-telephone utility) is unverified against the pinned corpus. Two pre-existing/unrelated things the fix did not settle: the five new derived rules use entity: Household while the four money rules stay entity: SnapUnit, and the parameter amounts were untouched. Follow-ups seen on this file: f2a9ab8e6 "Use corpus locators for Colorado SNAP sources" (provenance) and, after the monorepo absorption, 752ee8e28 "Reencode SNAP utility delegated settings", whose version retains all five derived eligibility rules and unifies every rule to entity: Household — evidence this commit's direction was the durable encoding.

verdict.justification: I resolved 10 CCR 2506-1 section 4.407.31 through the pinned corpus (us-co/regulation/10-ccr-2506-1/4.407.31, release us-rulespec-2026-07-22-current, corpus commit c5af5413) and the source does state the qualifying conditions the pre-fix module omitted: "A heating and cooling utility allowance (HCUA) is available only to households that: a. Incur or anticipate heating or cooling costs separate and apart from their rent or mortgage; b. Received a ... (LEAP) or ... (E-EBT) payment within the previous twelve (12) month period ...", plus (B)(1) "not entitled to the HCUA and that incur at least two (2) non-heating or non-cooling utility costs", (C)(1) "not entitled to the HCUA or BUA but is responsible for only one (1) ... The OUA is not allowed if the household's only utility expense is a telephone", and (D)(1) "households whose only utility cost is for a telephone". The pre-fix rules cited (A), (B), (C), (D) as their source and encoded none of those conditions, gating each allowance on an undeclared free input string (`snap_utility_allowance_type`, which appears nowhere else in the repo as a rule at the parent commit), so the encoded meaning disagreed with the cited text in both directions. The fix adds five derived rules that encode (A)(1)(a)-(e), (A)(2), the (B)-(D) utility count, and the HCUA/BUA precedence and telephone carve-out, then rewires all four allowance formulas onto them — adding clauses the source states, which is unrepresented_clause. I considered reclassifying to untraceable_branch (the `== "SUA"/"LUA"/"OUA"/"IUA"` codes are not Colorado's labels and have no basis in 4.407.31), but that dispatch was a placeholder standing in for the absent conditions rather than invented policy, and the bulk of the fix is the addition of the source's stated conditions.

verdict.notes: Source text verified, not inferred: resolved us-co/regulation/10-ccr-2506-1/4.407.31 from release us-rulespec-2026-07-22-current (corpus commit c5af541326e024e04cb533bbf5709ae04e6305f6, artifact data/corpus/provisions/us-co/regulation/2026-04-29-10-ccr-2506-1-r2026-07-15-self-contained.jsonl). Note the commit at 010774a5de predates the monorepo and has no .axiom/toolchain.toml, and the module header carries no corpus_citation_path (only a source_url to the CO SOS PDF), so release selection here was by scope search rather than a toolchain pin; the resolved body is the 2026-05-29 expression, one month after the 2026-05-01 fix, but it carries the same "Effective October 1, 2025" standards ($594/$377/$71/$97) the module encodes. Companion tests corroborate the meaning change: the old tests fed `snap_utility_allowance_type: SUA/LUA/OUA/IUA` directly, the new ones feed the six HCUA condition booleans and six utility-cost booleans, and the benefit-calculation test's expected allotment moves 182 -> 298 because the household now derives HCUA-eligible. Two residual items for a reviewer, neither changing the verdict: (1) the fix is partial coverage of 4.407.31 — (A)(3) ("The operation of a space heater ... do not qualify a household for the HCUA") and the shared-household full-allowance rules in (B)(2), (C)(2), (D)(1) are still unencoded, so an unrepresented_clause remainder persists; (2) the five new eligibility rules declare `entity: Household` while the four consuming allowance rules are `entity: SnapUnit`, a scope inconsistency introduced by this commit that is worth a separate look but is not the defect under review.

triage.commit_summary: This commit reworks the Barnsley working-age council tax reduction module that had been committed the same day in 598382330d: it re-anchors every proof-atom citation onto the correct corpus pages (page-51 -> page-52 for the Appendix 3 band table, page-10 -> page-11 for the 90% maximum, page-13 -> page-14 for the non-dependant deduction) and rewrites the protected-group logic so that protection is derived from qualifying disability income plus no earnings plus the applicant's own household-type Band 1 ceiling. The stated reason (PR #243) is the "sol semantic-fix harness" finding that protected-group entitlement uses per-household Band-1 ceilings, which the initial encode had collapsed to the single-person £98.05 figure for every household type.

modules.description_quote: protected-group per-household Band-1 ceilings (sol-corrected)
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The pre-fix encoding tested protected-group entitlement against the single-person Band 1 ceiling (barnsley_council_tax_reduction_single_band_1_upper_income_weekly, £98.05) for every household type, so a couple or family whose income fell within its own printed Band 1 ceiling (£153.92, £241.80, £329.68 on page 52) was wrongly denied the 90% protected rate and dropped to the ordinary 85%/70% ladder.
modules.triage_notes: Provision read through the pinned corpus release uk-rulespec-2026-08-04 (resolver, corpus commit 029f784d): page-52 carries Appendix 3, the four-column band table, and the sentence 'These are applicants who are in receipt of certain types of disability income49, have no earnings and fall within the band 1 income from the table above.' — 'the table above' is the per-household-type table, confirming the per-category ceilings. page-51 in the same release is unrelated text (second-adult gross income disregards), so the page-51->52 / 10->11 / 13->14 moves are genuine off-by-one citation re-anchoring; taken alone those are mechanical provenance, but the module also changes meaning, so the module is fidelity. Decisive semantic change: pre-fix `barnsley_council_tax_reduction_protected_group` was an opaque external input gated on the single ceiling; post-fix it is a derived rule `receives_qualifying_disability_income and has_no_earnings and weekly_assessed_income <= band_1_upper_income_weekly_by_household_category[household_income_category]`, with two new inputs and a new indexed parameter {0: 98.05, 1: 153.92, 2: 241.80, 3: 329.68} replacing the four scalar per-type Band 1 parameters. Behaviour change is confirmed by the companion test file: barnsley_ctr_protected_couple_below_ceiling (£153.91, disability income, no earnings) now expects protected_group holds and selected_support_rate 0.9, where the pre-fix module would have treated it as unprotected Band 1 at 0.85. The other changes in the same diff are behaviour-preserving refactors: support_rate_by_income_band 0 moved from 0.90 to 0 and band 5 removed while income_band's no-discount branch moved from 5 to 0 (net rate for a no-discount household is 0 both ways), protected 90% now flows through the new selected_support_rate rule instead of the old min(rate, maximum_support_rate) in the award formula (0.90 either way), and a band_4_code parameter was introduced. maximum_support_rate stays 0.90 — only its citation/excerpt moved, so the PR's '90% max' half of the finding was already correct pre-fix. Commit has exactly one module file; PR #243 has no reviews or review comments and the commit body contains only a Co-Authored-By trailer, so the PR body is the only stated reason. No follow-up commits touch this file (git log shows only 5983823 then 2d8fded). Kind alternative considered: wrong_entity_or_scope, since the single-person threshold was applied to couples and families; I chose amount_mismatch because the entity and population were right and the wrong thing was the threshold number used for three of the four household categories.

verdict.justification: The pre-fix protected-group gate read `if barnsley_council_tax_reduction_protected_group and barnsley_council_tax_reduction_weekly_assessed_income <= barnsley_council_tax_reduction_single_band_1_upper_income_weekly: 0`, applying the Single column's £98.05 Band-1 ceiling to every household category, while the pinned page-52 provision prints four Band-1 ceilings (£98.05 / £153.92 / £241.80 / £329.68) and says protected groups are those who "have no earnings and fall within the band 1 income from the table above." The fix replaces that scalar with `barnsley_council_tax_reduction_band_1_upper_income_weekly_by_household_category[...household_income_category]`, and the companion tests added in the same commit pin the changed outcome (`barnsley_ctr_protected_couple_at_ceiling`, income 153.92 → protected holds, selected_support_rate 0.9), which the pre-fix formula would have scored 0.85. So the threshold actually applied to couples and families was numerically wrong against the printed table — the encoding read the wrong table cell — which is amount_mismatch under the stated definition ("a numeric value, rate, threshold, table cell ... was wrong versus the source"). The rest of the diff (page-51→52 / 10→11 / 13→14 re-anchoring, excerpt expansion, band-code renumbering from {0 protected, 5 no-discount} to {0 no-discount} plus the new `selected_support_rate` indirection) is provenance and semantically neutral restructuring, so this is the one meaning change and it matches the first reader's reading.
verdict.quote: barnsley_council_tax_reduction_receives_qualifying_disability_income and barnsley_council_tax_reduction_has_no_earnings and barnsley_council_tax_reduction_weekly_assessed_income <= barnsley_council_tax_reduction_band_1_upper_income_weekly_by_household_category[barnsley_council_tax_reduction_household_income_category]
verdict.notes: Refutation attempts that failed: (1) "mechanical / restructure only" — rejected: the added test `barnsley_ctr_protected_couple_at_ceiling` (category 1, income 153.92) expects protected_group holds and rate 0.9, while the pre-fix formula gates on 153.92 <= 98.05 and would yield band 1 → 0.85; the meaning genuinely changed for 3 of 4 household categories. (2) "not_a_defect / new coverage" — rejected: all four Band-1 ceilings were already encoded pre-fix as `*_band_1_upper_income_weekly` parameters with correct values, and the ordinary band ladder already indexed by household category, so the module already claimed per-household banding; the protected gate simply used the wrong one. (3) "unrepresented_clause" — the fix does newly in-line `receives_qualifying_disability_income and has_no_earnings` (pre-fix these were delegated to an imported `protected_group` input, per the deferred_outputs reason), but that is a relocation of an already-represented condition, not a missing clause. The near-miss kind a reviewer should weigh is wrong_entity_or_scope: no literal number in the file was mis-transcribed, and the mechanism is "the single-person column applied to all household types," which is a parameter-selection error. I kept amount_mismatch because the rule's entity (Household), covered population, and outputs are unchanged pre and post; only the threshold value in force varies, and the taxonomy lists "threshold" and "table cell" explicitly under amount_mismatch. Source verified through the pinned release: corpus_release uk-rulespec-2026-08-04, provision record 03a6ef4e-c68f-522b-bf11-562a3864cdc0, resolved_text_sha256 782d0352…1699c3. Band-code renumbering check: pre band 5 → rate 0 and post band 0 → rate 0 are equivalent, and pre `min(rate, maximum_support_rate)` equals post `selected_support_rate` on both branches, so neither is a second defect.

triage.commit_summary: This squash-merge of PR #168 adds a brand-new 33-rule module encoding Coventry's 2026-27 working-age banded council tax reduction scheme (five excess-income bands at 80%/65%/40%/20%/0% applied to the §57 maximum reduction), plus its 11-case companion test, corpus manifest/provisions for the scheme PDF, and an oracle-coverage-pending entry. The PR body states it is a re-encode from scratch after a provision-role audit found the earlier staged Coventry module had encoded the out-of-scope pensioner classes; that earlier module was never merged, so relative to this commit's parent nothing is replaced — the repo had no Coventry policy files at all.

modules.description_quote: The module had encoded the maximum as 100% of the discounted annual liability less deductions, so every award was overstated by 25%.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: unclear: a genuine amount_mismatch existed inside the PR — the module computed the §57.1 maximum as 100% of the discounted annual liability less non-dependant deductions, omitting the statute's 'shall be 80 per cent' factor and overstating every award by 25% — but this commit's parent contains no Coventry module at all, so the merged diff carries only the already-corrected encoding and exposes no pre-fix state.
modules.triage_notes: Screen flag resolved: the file status here is 'added' and `git show e8870162:uk-coventry/policies/coventry/council-tax-reduction.yaml` fails ('exists on disk, but not in' the parent); `git ls-tree` shows no uk-coventry/policies files at the parent. The PR body confirms the earlier Coventry module 'was never merged - held out of #166 for exactly this reason', so this is NOT a re-encode replacing merged content. The defect the commit body describes is intra-PR: `gh api .../pulls/168/commits` lists ab709ad6db (initial encode) -> 8d80af4e08 (the 80% fix) -> e6a057783c. Both are present locally. The usable pre/post pair for a fidelity-judge corpus is 8d80af4e08 vs its parent ab709ad6db, where the module diff is exactly: formula `max(0, annual_council_tax_liability_after_statutory_discounts - annual_non_dependant_deductions)` -> `max(0, annual_council_tax_liability_after_statutory_discounts * maximum_reduction_liability_rate - annual_non_dependant_deductions)`, plus a new `maximum_reduction_liability_rate` parameter (0.80) and a proof atom on the 'shall be 80 per cent' span; the companion test file moved 800->640, 650->520, 400->320, 200->160, tariff 800->640, non-dep max 900->700 / award 720->560. I recommend re-anchoring this corpus entry to 8d80af4e08 and pruning the squash-merge SHA, since a judge given this commit's diff sees only correct content. Provision read: resolve_provision.py on uk-coventry/manual/council-tax-reduction-scheme-2026-2027/page-71 returns '57.1 Subject to paragraphs 57.2 to 57.4, the amount of a person's maximum council tax reduction in respect of a day for which he is liable to pay council tax, shall be 80 per cent, of the amount A divided by B', confirming 0.80 is right and 100% was wrong; kind is amount_mismatch (a rate wrong versus source) rather than unrepresented_clause because the fix changes the multiplier on an already-present maximum formula. Merged state verified correct: the merged test expectations are 640/520/320/160/0, tariff 640, non-dep max 700 / award 560. The description_quote is verbatim from the commit body with only the body's hard line wraps collapsed to single spaces. Only one review artifact exists (an issue comment from MaxGhenis reporting the Sol re-verdict); there are no formal PR reviews or review comments in the bundle. Sole module in the commit, so no multi-module pattern reuse.

verdict.justification: The first reader's premise is right about the squash-merge diff (2ad8f8025a adds the module against parent e887016, so no pre-fix state appears there) but its conclusion is refutable: the intra-PR fix commit 8d80af4e08 and its parent ab709ad6db are present in the local rulespec-uk repo, and `git show 8d80af4e08` exposes the exact pre/post pair — the formula changes from `max(0, annual_council_tax_liability_after_statutory_discounts - annual_non_dependant_deductions)` to the same expression multiplied by the new `maximum_reduction_liability_rate` parameter (0.80). The pinned corpus text for uk-coventry/.../page-71 reads "the amount of a person's maximum council tax reduction ... shall be 80 per cent, of the amount A divided by B ... less any deductions in respect of non-dependants", so the pre-fix encoding applied an implicit 100% rate where the source sets 80%, and the eleven recomputed companion expectations (award 800→640, 650→520, 400→320, 200→160, non-dep max 900→700) quantify the 25% overstatement. That is a rate wrong versus the source, i.e. amount_mismatch, not an ambiguous or merely additive change.

-          max(0, annual_council_tax_liability_after_statutory_discounts - annual_non_dependant_deductions)
+          max(0, annual_council_tax_liability_after_statutory_discounts * maximum_reduction_liability_rate - annual_non_dependant_deductions)

The usable pre/post pair is commit 8d80af4e0856aeeaaa1c5d1354af21a011842365 ("Encode the §57.1 80% maximum-liability rate (Sol review finding)"), parent ab709ad6db, path uk-coventry/policies/coventry/council-tax-reduction.yaml (+24/-1 module, +17/-27 companion test). Also note the fix commit's proof atom cites page-71 while the module header's corpus_citation_path is page-114 (Schedule 2 band table); both resolve cleanly under release uk-rulespec-2026-07-24, and page-71 is the correct §57.1 anchor for the rate.

item.subject: (screen-flagged) Missing boundary in the merged GOV.UK student-loan repayment module: body says it "never capped the annual repayment at the borrower's outstanding balance"; adds min(scheduled_deduction, balance) cap and grounds it (closes #77).
item.screen_reason: Missing boundary in the merged GOV.UK student-loan repayment module: body says it "never capped the annual repayment at the borrower's outstanding balance"; adds min(scheduled_deduction, balance) cap and grounds it (closes #77).

triage.commit_summary: The commit adds a cap to the GOV.UK student-loan-repayments encoding so that the annual `student_loan_repayment` is `min(scheduled_deduction, outstanding_balance)` when the borrower's outstanding balance is supplied, via a new optional `outstanding_student_loan_balance` input gated by `outstanding_student_loan_balance_is_known` (absent by default, preserving the old scheduled-deduction result). It was made because the encoding modelled only the 9%/6%-over-threshold scheduled deduction and never reflected the GOV.UK rule that repayments stop once the loan is repaid in full, which produced 43 near-end-of-loan mismatches against the EFRS oracle comparison; the same commit adds the second corpus citation (getting-a-refund), an upstream_source_check against SI 2009/470, two new proof atoms, and three companion tests.

modules.description_quote:
The GOV.UK student-loan-repayments encoding modelled the scheduled income-
contingent deduction (9% over threshold for Plans 1/2/4/5, 6% for
Postgraduate) but never capped the annual repayment at the borrower's
outstanding balance.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The pre-fix formula returned the full scheduled income-contingent deduction (rate x income over threshold) with no upper bound, so for a borrower whose remaining balance was smaller than that deduction it reported a repayment larger than the amount still owed, contradicting the cited GOV.UK provision that HMRC stops repayments once the loan is repaid in full and refunds anything paid over the total owed.
modules.triage_notes: Single-module commit; only this module file, its companion .test.yaml, and the encoding manifest changed. Provision WAS read through the pinned corpus release (uk/guidance/govuk/student-loan-repayments/getting-a-refund, 482 chars): 'You can ask for a refund if you have paid more than the total amount you owe. HM Revenue and Customs will tell your employer to stop taking repayments from your salary when you have repaid your loan in full...' — this supports the cap on the net annual repayment. Caveat a reviewer should know: the same provision says salary deductions 'can take around four weeks to stop, so you may pay back more than you owe', so the source describes over-deduction-then-refund rather than a hard in-year deduction cap; the encoding models the net-of-refund amount. Second caveat: the cap is gated on a new optional input defaulting to absent, so the module's output is unchanged for callers that do not supply a balance — this is why one could argue the change adds new scope; I still classify it fidelity because the module's claimed output (annual student loan repayment) was overstated near end of loan and the fix cites source text for the missing clause (the commit reports 43 dispositioned EFRS mismatches becoming raw matches). The same commit also made provenance-only changes bundled with the fidelity fix: corpus_citation_path -> corpus_citation_paths (adding getting-a-refund), a new module.source_verification.upstream_source_check block citing SI 2009/470 Sch 1A and Part 6, an updated module summary, an updated `source:` string on the rule, and two new proof atoms (kind: exception and kind: condition) on versions[0].formula. Downstream alias rule `student_loan_repayments` was not edited but inherits the cap since its formula is just `student_loan_repayment`. Screen flag called this a 'missing boundary', but the defect is a missing cap clause, not a wrong comparison strictness or direction, so unrepresented_clause rather than boundary_direction. PR #86 has no reviews or review comments; PR body restates the commit message.

verdict.justification: The diff changes encoded meaning: the `student_loan_repayment` formula gains a source-grounded upper bound `min(scheduled_deduction, max(0, outstanding_student_loan_balance))` that the pre-fix formula lacked entirely, and the module adds `getting-a-refund` as a citation path with two new proof atoms labeled `kind: exception` and `kind: condition`. I resolved that provision through the pinned release and both excerpts are verbatim, including "HM Revenue and Customs will tell your employer to stop taking repayments from your salary when you have repaid your loan in full" — a clause the source states and the encoding did not represent at all, which is exactly `unrepresented_clause`. I tried `boundary_direction` (the screen text says "missing boundary") and rejected it: no pre-existing comparison had its strictness or direction reversed, a whole clause was absent. I also tried `not_a_defect` on the grounds that the cap is gated behind a new optional input defaulting to absent, but no new output surface was added and needing a new input is the ordinary cost of representing a previously absent clause.
verdict.quote: +          if listed_student_loan_plan_applies: if outstanding_student_loan_balance_is_known: min(student_loan_repayment_rate * max(0, annual_income_before_tax_and_other_deductions - student_loan_annual_income_threshold), max(0, outstanding_student_loan_balance)) else: student_loan_repayment_rate * max(0, annual_income_before_tax_and_other_deductions - student_loan_annual_income_threshold) else: 0
verdict.notes:
Two refutation attempts, both survived, but a reviewer should see the caveats.

(1) The strongest counter-evidence is in the cited provision itself. Resolved `uk/guidance/govuk/student-loan-repayments/getting-a-refund` (corpus release `uk-rulespec-2026-07-12`, corpus commit 3cc9219a, provision file sha 91208a85, line 11, body sha ab400b5a). Full text: "You can ask for a refund if you have paid more than the total amount you owe. HM Revenue and Customs will tell your employer to stop taking repayments from your salary when you have repaid your loan in full, but salary deductions can take around four weeks to stop, so you may pay back more than you owe." The source therefore explicitly contemplates the gross PAYE deduction EXCEEDING the outstanding balance, with a refund as the remedy. This contradicts the commit body's flat assertion "A borrower never repays more than they still owe". It does not rescue the pre-fix formula, because the rule is `period: Year` with `period_kind: tax_year` and the refund makes the annual amount borne equal to min(scheduled, balance), but the fix's own framing overstates the source. A reviewer grading the commit message against the provision should note this.

(2) The pre-fix module cited ONLY `uk/guidance/govuk/student-loan-repayments/what-you-pay`, whose resolved text (body sha 87b95b8c) contains no stop-at-full-repayment language — only thresholds, the 9%/6% rates, and Self Assessment. So the fix expands the module's source scope to a provision it had not previously cited, rather than correcting a formula against the provision it did cite. Combined with the cap being gated behind a new `outstanding_student_loan_balance_is_known` input that defaults to false (all four pre-existing tests were amended to set it false and their expected outputs are unchanged), no previously-expressible scenario changes value. This is the residual argument for downgrading to `unclear`; I did not take it because the module's claimed output surface (`student_loan_repayment`, "GOV.UK student loan repayment amount") is unchanged and is what the clause bounds.

(3) Supporting evidence of real wrong outputs, not just added precision: the PR states the companion axiom-oracles bridge change "converts the 43 dispositioned near-end-of-loan mismatches in the `uk-tax-benefits-efrs` comparison from `bridge_artifact` to raw matches". Note those 43 had been dispositioned as bridge artifacts, i.e. previously treated as an input-availability issue rather than an encoding error — a reviewer may read that either way.

(4) Nothing mechanical-only here: module file is +37/-4 with a real formula rewrite. The commit also touches only the companion test file and `.axiom/encoding-manifests/`. No PR reviews or comments exist to quote.

(5) Kind alternatives considered and rejected: amount_mismatch (no numeric literal changed — thresholds 26900/29385/33795/25000/21000 and rates 9%/6% are untouched), wrong_period_or_effective_date (effective_from stays '2026-04-06'), wrong_entity_or_scope (entity Person, unchanged), polarity_or_logic (no boolean inversion; the new `if/else` is additive gating).

item.subject: (screen-flagged) Unsure: adds a 2026-04-06 version to the already-merged SSCBA 1992 s.13 Class 3 module, which until then carried only the 2025-26 rate ("still GBP 17.75, the 2025-26 figure"), so 2026-27 weeks returned a stale amount; body frames it as "currency/completeness only" but it is a wrong-amount-for-period correction of a merged module.
item.screen_reason: Unsure: adds a 2026-04-06 version to the already-merged SSCBA 1992 s.13 Class 3 module, which until then carried only the 2025-26 rate ("still GBP 17.75, the 2025-26 figure"), so 2026-27 weeks returned a stale amount; body frames it as "currency/completeness only" but it is a wrong-amount-for-period correction of a merged module.

triage.commit_summary: The commit appends a second version (effective_from 2026-04-06, formula 18.40) to the class_3_weekly_contribution_amount parameter in the already-merged SSCBA 1992 s.13 module, because the s.13(1) base text on legislation.gov.uk is unconsolidated and still reads £17.75 (the 2025-26 rate), so the new version is grounded to the GOV.UK "Rates and allowances: National Insurance contributions" guidance (block-11/block-13) newly ingested as axiom-corpus#222, with the module's source_verification extended to the guidance paths plus an upstream_source_check rationale and the corpus pin bumped to 3ecec6d. Two companion tests were added to pin the version boundary (first 2026-27 tax week at 18.40, final 2025-26 week at 17.75); the maintainer frames the change as "currency/completeness only" with no oracle affected.

modules.description_quote: The s.13(1) base text on legislation.gov.uk still reads "shall be £17.75" (the 2025-26 figure) — the annual administrative re-rating is not consolidated into the statute text
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: unclear: the pre-fix module carried a single open-ended version (effective_from 2025-04-06, no effective_to) at 17.75, so it returned the 2025-26 figure for 2026-27 tax weeks whose official HMRC rate is 18.40 — but 17.75 is exactly what its only cited source, the unconsolidated s.13(1) text, says, and the 2026-27 guidance was not in the corpus at the module's pre-fix pin.
modules.triage_notes: Read the provision through the pinned corpus release: s.13(1) as expressed reads "subject to the following provisions of this section, the amount of a Class 3 contribution shall be £17.75", and s.13(4)-(7) presuppose that the amount varies by tax year ("the amount of a Class 3 contribution applicable at the time of payment differs from..."), but the statute text nowhere states 18.40. Timing argues FOR a real defect: the module was first merged 2026-07-06 in rulespec-uk#82 (git log on the file: 6346345 -> f7184e0), i.e. three months AFTER the 2026-04-06 uprating, so as merged it returned a stale amount for the then-current tax year, and the new companion test class_3_contribution_uses_uprated_weekly_rate_from_6_april_2026 would have failed against the pre-fix module. Timing argues AGAINST: the fix does not change any previously encoded number, effective date or formula — it only appends versions[1] — and the correcting value comes from a source (GOV.UK rates guidance, block-11/block-13) that was only ingested in axiom-corpus#222 and pinned in this same commit (toolchain axiom_corpus_ref 6bc9344 -> 3ecec6d), so a fidelity judge comparing the pre-fix module against its cited corpus source would correctly find agreement; the maintainer's stated reason is explicitly "currency/ completeness only", not a mis-encoding. Best fit if promoted to fidelity is wrong_period_or_effective_date under 'timeless encoding of superseded text' (the sole open-ended version claimed all periods from 2025-04-06 onward); amount_mismatch is a defensible alternate kind since the wrong output is a wrong rate for the 2026-27 period. The commit also makes non-fidelity changes in the same file: source_verification migrates from a single corpus_citation_path to corpus_citation_paths plus an upstream_source_check block, the rule's free-text `source:` string and the module summary prose are rewritten, and four proof atoms are added for versions[1] — all provenance/metadata, mechanical on their own. No PR reviews or review comments exist on PR #85 (empty reviews/review_comments/issue_comments), so no reviewer characterization is available. Single-module chunk; the only other files are the companion test file and .axiom/toolchain.toml. Later commit 0644db8 (2026-07-13, canonical-layout hard cut, #133) also touches this path but is a layout/binding change, not a fidelity follow-up.

verdict.justification: The change is strictly additive: versions[0] (2025-04-06, 17.75) and its proof atom are byte-identical across the diff, no effective_to, formula, input, output, or scope was altered, and the only substantive addition is a new versions[1] grounded in a GOV.UK guidance page that `git diff --name-only 6bc9344..3ecec6d` in axiom-corpus shows was first ingested by corpus#222 in this very commit — so at the pre-fix pin the corpus contained no text stating the 2026-27 amount. Reading s.13(1) through the pinned release confirms the cited source still says "the amount of a Class 3 contribution shall be £17.75" with no temporal qualifier even at expression date 2026-06-01, so the pre-fix encoding did not disagree with its cited source text; it is faithful-but-stale relative to the world, which the commit itself labels "currency/completeness only". The 2025-04-06 effective_from is a module-wide convention (the two pure-condition rules in the same file carry the identical date), so it is not an asserted rate-specific boundary the encoder then failed to close. This is annual-uprating coverage enabled by a corpus ingest, not a correction of encoded meaning against the source.
verdict.quote:
versions:
       - effective_from: '2025-04-06'
         formula: |-
           17.75
+      - effective_from: '2026-04-06'
+        formula: |-
+          18.40
verdict.notes:
Refutation basis, verified this session: (1) axiom-corpus 6bc9344..3ecec6d adds exactly one source tree, data/corpus/sources/uk/guidance/2026-07-05-uk-national-insurance-rates/..., i.e. the block-11/block-13 guidance did not exist at the pre-fix pin; (2) resolve_provision on uk/statute/ukpga/1992/4/13 returns "the amount of a Class 3 contribution shall be £17.75" at expression_date 2026-06-01 — the statute expression is unamended and untimed, so nothing in the corpus made the open-ended version wrong; (3) the diff touches no pre-existing value, date, formula, input, output, or scope.

Strongest surviving counter-argument a pruning reviewer should weigh: behaviorally the module DID answer 2026-27 weeks (open-ended version, period Week) and returned 17.75 where HMRC's rate is 18.40, and the new companion test class_3_contribution_uses_uprated_weekly_rate_from_6_april_2026 asserts 18.40, so runtime output changed for periods the module already claimed. If the corpus's standard is "encoded meaning vs the law in force" rather than "encoded meaning vs the cited corpus text", this reads as wrong_period_or_effective_date under the "timeless encoding of superseded text" clause. I did not adopt that because the supersession (the re-rating order substituting the s.13(1) figure) is not present anywhere in the corpus at either pin, and the statute's current legislation.gov.uk expression still reads £17.75.

Against the first reader's kind: even if kept as a defect, note the fix bounds nothing — no effective_to was added and 17.75 remains correct for its own period — so the corrective act is adding a period's value, which sits awkwardly between wrong_period_or_effective_date and amount_mismatch. That ambiguity is itself a reason this case is weak benchmark material: there is no pre-fix source text a reader could have compared against to catch it.

item.subject: (screen-flagged) 'retire' verb: signed retirement of five PolicyEngine model wrappers (child-benefit, universal-credit, housing-benefit, esa-income, severe-disablement-allowance) because "their legal content lives in the statute and regulation modules"; source-grounding retirement of model-grounded modules.
item.screen_reason: 'retire' verb: signed retirement of five PolicyEngine model wrappers (child-benefit, universal-credit, housing-benefit, esa-income, severe-disablement-allowance) because "their legal content lives in the statute and regulation modules"; source-grounding retirement of model-grounded modules.

triage.commit_summary: The commit ran `axiom-encode retire` to delete five "PolicyEngine-alignment" wrapper modules (child benefit, ESA income, housing benefit, severe disablement allowance, universal credit) along with their companion test files, writing a signed retirement manifest for each and bumping the toolchain pin from axiom-encode 0.2.621 to 0.2.647. The stated reason is that these surfaces encoded PolicyEngine microsimulation constructs — take-up gates and `reported_*` survey inputs — and were grounded on provisions that do not state what the formulas computed, while their genuine legal content already lives in the statute and regulation modules.

modules.description_quote: This PolicyEngine-alignment surface returns the weekly Child Benefit amount received by a family: the section 141 weekly entitlement if the family would claim Child Benefit, and nil otherwise.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The formula gated the s.141 weekly entitlement on a module-local `would_claim_child_benefit` take-up input and cited s.141 as the proof basis for that condition, but SSCBA 1992 s.141 entitles a person responsible for a child or qualifying young person to child benefit and says nothing about whether a family would claim it.
modules.triage_notes: Deletion, not an in-place edit: the whole module (36 lines) and its companion test were removed by `axiom-encode retire`; a fidelity judge must score the pre-fix file. Provision read through the pinned corpus (uk-legislation-pilot, corpus commit 66dcb07): s.141 text is purely the entitlement rule, and the proof atom excerpt "entitled to child benefit" is a paraphrase, not verbatim in the provision ("shall be entitled ... to a benefit (to be known as \"child benefit\")"). Entity was Family though s.141 entitles a person. The test file confirms `would_claim_child_benefit` was a module-local unsourced input. Maintainer framing in PR #44 comments: MaxGhenis calls these "the biggest \"derived from another model rather than from law\" debt in the UK corpus"; nikhilwoodruff describes the removed pattern as "PolicyEngine-alignment surface... used by PolicyEngine UK and HBAI", `reported_*` inputs". The retire manifest (.axiom/encoding-manifests/policies/govuk/child-benefit.json, not an allowed quote_source) records reason: "PolicyEngine model wrappers retired from the rules registry: survey/take-up constructs are consumer concerns; legal content lives in the statute and regulation modules". Module never re-added: no policies/govuk/child-benefit.yaml in rulespec-uk HEAD. Residual doubt (applies to all five): retirement-by-deletion could be read as a scope/dedup decision rather than a meaning correction, hence confidence below 0.8.

modules.description_quote: This PolicyEngine-alignment surface returns the annual income-related Employment and Support Allowance amount used by PolicyEngine UK and HBAI: reported income-related ESA reduced by annual tariff income when the benefit unit passes PolicyEngine's income-related ESA eligibility gate, and nil otherwise.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The formula subtracted a tariff-income term from a survey `reported_income_related_esa_for_year` input behind PolicyEngine's own eligibility gate and grounded all of it on ESA Regs 2008 reg 118, which only deems capital above GBP 6,000 (or GBP 10,000) to be weekly income of GBP 1 per complete GBP 250 and never defines an award amount or any subtraction from a reported receipt.
modules.triage_notes: Same retirement pattern as index 0 (whole module plus test deleted by `axiom-encode retire`). Provision read: reg 118 (SI 2008/794) is 'Calculation of tariff income from capital' — its excerpts quoted in the proof atoms are genuine, but they support a means-test income computation, not the module's award formula; tariff income is treated as income in the means test, not deducted from the benefit paid. The `income_related_esa_eligible` gate and the `reported_*` base are model constructs with no provision behind them — exactly the pattern nikhilwoodruff names in the PR comments ("`reported_*` inputs"). Not re-added at HEAD.

modules.description_quote: This PolicyEngine-alignment surface returns the annual Housing Benefit amount used by PolicyEngine UK and HBAI: annual Housing Benefit before the benefit cap, less the annual benefit-cap reduction, floored at nil when the benefit unit would claim Housing Benefit, and nil otherwise.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: A Housing Benefit output was grounded entirely on Universal Credit Regulations 2013 reg 80A — which only divides the UC benefit-cap annual limit by 12 and defines Greater-London residence for the UC cap — and was gated on an unsourced `would_claim_housing_benefit` take-up input, so neither the cap subtraction nor the claiming condition has any basis in the cited provision.
modules.triage_notes: Same retirement pattern as index 0. Provision read: uk/regulation/uksi/2013/376/80A resolves to the UC benefit-cap 'relevant amount' rule; its only mention of housing benefit is the Greater-London residence test ("the claimant is in receipt of housing benefit in respect of a dwelling ... in Greater London"), so the proof excerpt "claimant receives housing benefit" is a paraphrase, not verbatim, and is repurposed as the take-up condition. Housing Benefit's own cap rules live in the Housing Benefit Regulations, not SI 2013/376 — wrong-provision grounding, which the kind list places under untraceable_branch (a wrong_entity_or_scope reading is also defensible since the module computes an HB amount from a UC provision). Not re-added at HEAD.

modules.description_quote: This PolicyEngine-alignment surface returns the annual Severe Disablement Allowance amount used by PolicyEngine UK and HBAI: the maximum weekly Severe Disablement Allowance rate, annualized for people with reported SDA receipt, and nil otherwise.
modules.pre_fix_wrong_because: The module paid everyone whose `reported_severe_disablement_allowance_for_year > 0` the maximum weekly rate times 52, a branch keyed on a survey input rather than any statutory condition, and the 52 was grounded on UC Regs 2013 Sch 4 para 7, a renter monthly-equivalent rule whose text is "weekly payments are multiplied by 52 and divided by 12".
modules.triage_notes: Strongest of the five and the clearest wrong-provision grounding. Both provisions read: SI 2013/376 Sch 4 para 7 is about calculating renters' relevant payments as a monthly amount under Universal Credit, nothing to do with annualizing SDA, and the proof excerpt truncates the sentence to "weekly payments are multiplied by 52", dropping "and divided by 12" and thereby changing its meaning; the rule's own `source:` field names the Social Security (Claims and Payments) Regulations 1987, which is not the cited corpus path. SI 2026/148 Sch 1 does carry "Severe disablement allowance, GBP 103.85" and the age-related additions, but the addition is cited as a proof atom while never entering the formula, and the flat max rate ignores rate variation. Two rules in one file; the parameter rule (rules[severe_disablement_allowance_weeks_in_year].versions[0].formula) is the second decisive path.
